body:
OBJECTIVES
- Students explain why a fraction a/b is equivalent to (n × a)/(n × b) using visual fraction models, and generate equivalent fractions (4.NF.A.1).
- Students compare two fractions with different numerators and denominators by creating common denominators or numerators or by comparing to a benchmark such as 1/2, record comparisons with >, = or <, and recognize that comparisons are valid only when the fractions refer to the same whole (4.NF.A.2).

MATERIALS
- Paper fraction strips (halves, thirds, fourths, sixths, eighths, tenths, twelfths), one set per student
- Grid paper or blank rectangles for area models
- A number line from 0 to 1 on the board
- Colored pencils

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read Same Amount, Different Names. Students fold a paper strip in half, then in half again, and again, recording 1/2 = 2/4 = 4/8. Lesson: Modeling Equivalent Fractions.
Day 2: Assignment: Fraction Strips. Partners line up strips to prove each answer before writing it. Share: what rule do the strips show?
Day 3: Comparing fractions mini-lesson: three strategies (benchmark 1/2, same denominator, same numerator). Assignment: Which Is Greater?
Day 4: Finish Which Is Greater? Number line talk: place 1/3, 5/12, 1/4, 1/2 and 3/4 on one line. Discuss Mia's pizza problem: why the whole matters.
Day 5: Assessment: Fraction Check. Fraction strips are allowed.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: keep fraction strips out for every problem; start with halves, fourths and eighths before thirds, sixths and twelfths.
- Support: give a multiplication chart to find common denominators.
- Stretch: find all the fractions equivalent to 3/4 with a denominator less than 30, and explain the pattern.
- Multilingual learners: post numerator, denominator, equivalent and benchmark with a labeled picture. Let students prove answers with strips and gestures before writing explanations, and offer frames such as "___ is greater than ___ because ___."

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
This unit we are learning that different fractions can name the same amount: 1/2 of a sandwich is the same as 2/4 of it. Your child is bringing home paper fraction strips; please keep them in the homework folder. At home, try cutting a sandwich or a tortilla in half, then into fourths, and ask: did the amount change? Which is more, 1/3 or 1/4 of the same sandwich?
title: Teacher guide: Equivalent Fractions
